title: ばかり — “nothing but ～ / only ～”
summary: ばかり shows that the same thing happens again and again, or that there is only that one kind of thing: ‘nothing but ～’. It often carries a critical or surprised feeling. It follows a noun or a verb て-form + いる.

patterns.gloss: noun + ばかり + verb (ゲームばかりしている)
te-form + ばかりいる: keeps doing only that (寝てばかりいる)

body.p: Put ばかり after a noun, where を, が, or の would be dropped: ゲームをする → ゲームばかりする. With a verb, use the て-form: 寝てばかりいる (does nothing but sleep).
ばかり often means the speaker finds the amount or bias excessive: 甘い物ばかり食べている (eats nothing but sweets). It tends to be critical, so be careful when talking about others.
だけ simply states ‘only’ in a neutral way. ばかり adds the sense of ‘again and again’ or ‘too many’, so it is more emotional. 食べたばかり (verb た-form + ばかり) is a different use meaning ‘just ate’.

examples.ja: 弟（おとうと）はゲームばかりしています。
examples.romaji: Otōto wa gēmu bakari shite imasu.
examples.tr: My little brother does nothing but play games.
examples.note: ゲームをする → ゲームばかりする.

examples.ja: 妹（いもうと）は甘（あま）い物（もの）ばかり食（た）べている。
examples.romaji: Imōto wa amai mono bakari tabete iru.
examples.tr: My little sister eats nothing but sweets.
examples.note: を is dropped before ばかり.

examples.ja: 友（とも）だちは同（おな）じ歌（うた）ばかり聞（き）いている。
examples.romaji: Tomodachi wa onaji uta bakari kiite iru.
examples.tr: My friend listens to nothing but the same song.

pitfalls: Drop を/が before ばかり: ゲームばかりする, not ゲームをばかりする.
It sounds critical. To state a neutral fact, だけ is safer.
